10044958:
Anne Terry East Pond Association LD 1435
To whom it may concern:
I am the Secretary of the East Pond Association, where we have an IF&W-owned public boat launch located in the town of Oakland.
Our lake association funds the Courtesy Boat Inspection staffing at this boat launch during the times of year that experience the most boat traffic. We do this via a combination of volunteer hours and paid staff hours with costs covered by fundraising from our members as well as grants from the towns of Smithfield and Oakland.
I've spent my life on this lake, and I am the second generation in my family to serve on the East Pond Association Board. In that time, I've seen the challenges the lake faces change over the years- and, if anything, expand to include new risks. As the priorities have changed, the East Pond Association and 7 Lakes Alliance have been at the forefront of educating residents and visitors to our lake about what people need to do to show up in ways that are lake-friendly. Off the top of my head, this has included:
 Checking boats for millfoil before entering the lake  Identifying and reporting curly-leaf pondweed, a highly invasive aquatic plant, which was
spotted in our lake in 2021  Raising funds to cover a $1.2M alum treatment to combat algae blooms in 2018, and
promoting practices and changes to prevent phosphorous-laden runoff into the lake from local commercial and residential properties, as well as roads.  Education about wake zones to prevent erosion  Following Audubon's best practices to support the dwindling loon population on the lake
We support this via a combination of printed brochures, meetings, advocacy, and much more. In all cases, prevention is much more cost-effective than remediation, and public compliance is critical to that. This was made all the more challenging- particularly for day visitors- by the removal of an information kiosk at our boat launch by IF&W as well as a professionally constructed sign educating boat launch users about curly leaf pondweed.
I strongly support LD 1435 which will restore this critical education infrastructure. Right now, for day visitors in particular, unless there is a Courtesy Boat Inspector (CBI) present, there is no way for us to provide education about lake-friendly practices. Not only is it cost-prohibitive for us to staff the boat launch 24/7 during the entire season, the absence of a kiosk makes the education provided by the CBIs less likely to be fully understood and taken seriously. And given that the conservation priorities can vary from lake to lake and year to year on a given lake, providing ample space to the lake associations and other local conservation organizations such as 7 Lakes Alliance will result in the most up to date and lake-specific information being shared.

Testimony of Rep. Bill Bridgeo introducing
LD 1435, An Act to Allow a Municipality or Locally Recognized Lake
Association to Post Certain Information on the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife's Information Kiosks Located at State Boat Launch
Facilities
Before the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee
Good aftemoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and distinguished colleagues of the
Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee. My name is Bill Bridgeo, and I represent House District 60, which is part of Augusta. I am here today to introduce LD 1435, An Act to Allow a
Municipality or Locally Recognized Lake Association to Post Certain Information on the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife's Information Kiosks Located at State Boat Launch Facilities.
LD 1435, if enacted, will provide local recognized lake associations with the opportunity to post, on IF&W kiosks, important information about their mission, ongoing efforts to protect lake water
quality, contact information and cautionary information aimed at reducing the risks associated with aquatic invasive species like milfoil.
Typically, IF&W kiosks are fairly large structures and this bill contemplates that only a small
section of the display space (perhaps the size of an 8 `/2 x ll-inch piece of paper) of that area
would be made available to a properly vetted lake association.
I'm not concerned about the potential "slippery slope" concerns the Department may have. I
think they can address that with routine rules. The kiosks need not become community bulletin
boards.
I am passionate that the primary lake protection entities on our treasured 6,200 lakes and ponds
have some access to the most obvious and prominent messaging opportunities to get the word
out about their existence and how to help them.
Thank you for your consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you have for me.

10046586:
Diana McLaughlin WAYNE LD 1435
I am writing in strong support of LD 1435. As a Board member of both the 30 Mile River Watershed Association and the Lovejoy Pond Improvement Association, I am aware of the importance of educating users of lakes and ponds about watershed protection issues. For example, Androscoggin Lake, located in the 30 Mile River Watershed, has an invasive milfoil infestation near the heavily used state boat launch, and has been declining in water quality in recent years with severe algal blooms occurring each summer. It is critical for municipalities and local watershed protection organizations to be able to inform boaters of specific threats to lakes and ponds, and inform them on how they can (and must) help in efforts to mitigate these problems, such as avoiding transporting plant materials into a lake and keeping their boat away from infested areas. IF&W kiosks at state boat launches are a perfect place to post such information, and I urge the Committee to allow municipalities and appropriate organizations to do so. Respectfully, Diana McLaughlin
190345:
TESTIMONY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
In Opposition to L.D. 1435
"An Act to Allow a Municipality or Locally Recognized Lake Association to
Post Certain Information on the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife's Information Kiosks Located at State Boat Launch Facilities"
DATE OF HEARING: Wednesday, April 16, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee. I am Diano Circo, Chief Planner at the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
(IFW), speaking on behalf of the Department in opposition to L.D. 1435.
This bill requires the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife to provide reasonable space to display information on the department's informational kiosks located at state boat launch facilities to municipalities and local lake associations and similar nonprofit organizations and disseminate to the general public information about these associations and organizations and water quality and invasive
species activities.
The Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife manages 182 water access facilities across the state to provide fair and equitable public access to Maine's waters for fishing and boating. All of the Department's
facilities are acquired, developed, or maintained utilizing federal funds.
Standardized and concise signage across all Department facilities is essential for clear, accurate, and
effective messaging. Previously, the Department maintained informational kiosks at many of its water
access sites. However, these kiosks became costly and difficult to maintain and frequently became collection points for cluttered, incorrect, or misleading information. Given the large number of sites managed by the Department, effectively regulating the content placed in these kiosks was nearly impossible, resulting in chaotic and ineflective messaging. As a result, the Department has actively worked over the past several years to remove these kiosks to address these issues.
Currently, our signage prioritizes essential information such as site use rules, state boating and fishing regulations, aquatic invasive species prevention (Clean, Drain, Dry), and required notices from funding sources like the Sport Fish Restoration Program and Land for Maine's Future.
In 2023, aquatic invasive species signage was thoughtfully developed through a legislative-directed interageney task force. This task force included broad stakeholder representation from lake associations, watercraft owner groups, educational programs, marinas, municipalities, sporting associations, and
outdoor recreation organizations.

The Department engages in extensive outreach and education efforts statewide to raise awareness about the importance of preventing the spread of aquatic invasive species. These initiatives include partnerships with stakeholder groups, public information campaigns, workshops, educational materials, and direct community engagement to effectively communicate best practices and prevention strategies. Additionally, the Department utilizes consistent and unified messaging developed by the interagency task force to ensure accuracy and effectiveness.
The Department frequently receives additional requests from diverse entities including lake and watershed associations, fishing and hunting groups, municipalities, businesses, and conservation
organizations to install their signs at our facilities. Additionally, we routinely find numerous unauthorized
signs that are inaccurate, misleading, or contradictory to Department policies. Allowing proliferation of signs leads to "sign fatigue," diminishing the effectiveness of critical messaging and overwhelming visitors with excessive and conflicting information.
Due to these challenges, the Department established a clear signage policy limiting signs and messaging
dissemination exclusively to those developed and installed by the Department. Allowing individual organizations or businesses to use federally and state-funded public facilities for advertising, advocacy, fundraising, or requiring the Department to distribute their organizational messaging raises significant policy concerns and questions regarding the appropriate use of public resources for private benefit. Furthermore, setting such a precedent could rapidly become overwhelming and exceedingly difficult for the Department to effectively manage.
For these reasons, the Department opposes this bill and respectfully urges the Committee to carefully consider the impacts of sign fatigue and information overload on the effectiveness of vital communications at our facilities.
I would be pleased to answer any questions at this time or during the work session.

10044850:
Edith Cornwall East Pond Association LD 1435
I, Edith Cornwall, am the President of the East Pond Association located in Oakland, ME. where we have an IF&W owned public boat launch. We provide Courtesy Boat Inspection (CBI) at the boat launch by paid and volunteer inspectors beginning Memorial Day Weekend for 12 hours per day Friday, Saturday, Sunday, all holidays and for fishing tournaments. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday are covered for 8 hours through Labor Day with limited hours until Indigenous Peoples Weekend. Our anticipated expenses for 2025 are over $22,000.
In 2021 Curly-leaf Pondweed, a highly aggressive invasive was found. The DEP designated this as a Rapid Response Plan and this will be the 4th year that the7 Lakes Alliance Dive Team has diligently pulled plants from May until late in the fall.
IF&W removed the boat launch kiosk as well as a professionally constructed sign showing a picture of Curly-leaf Pondweed, the location of the infestation and a request that boaters avoid the infested area. In order to educate the public and to gain their cooperation, our association designed and printed 1,000 brochures which are distributed in public locations and by the CBIs. I have personally spoken at public meetings in order to educate groups about this infestation and to explain how we are working to prevent this from invading the remaining 6 Belgrade Lakes.
A 2 phase Alum treatment costing $1.2 million was done in 2018. The East Pond Association promotes the education of Best Management Practices, buffers, road maintenance, the Adopt-A-Shore Program, Loon responsibility, safety and lake preservation. We all know that REMEDIATION IS WAY MORE COSTLY THAN PREVENTION.
There are many new things to learn once you decide to live on a lake. Education is key to good decision making thus a kiosk is one of our most valuable educational assets. Unfortunately, we are not allowed to build a kiosk on IF&W own property.
I strongly support LD 1435 which will bring back this crucial educational structure. I also request that you consider providing more space for posting Lake Association materials. We, the Lake Associations, are the people who work on a day to day basis educating the year round and seasonal residents.
Please help us accomplish our goal of "Keeping East Pond Picture Perfect".
